sm: Georgia Howe opens the show with the day's headlines: a Justice Department scam crackdown and a planned military explosion in Iowa. The main story is a fight inside the Republican Party over immigration after the party's heavy midterm losses. Daily Wire reporter Megan Basham explains that Oklahoma Governor Kevin Stitt wants President Trump to spend his last two years seeking a bipartisan deal with legal status pathways and more employer say over workers. Ann Coulter calls this short-sighted and driven by donors who want cheap labor. Florida Republican Maria Salazar and Texas Democrat Veronica Escobar back the Dignity Act, which would let about 10 million long-term immigrants stay legally if they pay restitution and pass background checks. Co-lead Mark Stutzman says mass deportation is not workable. Hugh Hewitt urged Trump to pardon over a million immigrants, and National Review called that amnesty for nothing. Basham says Trump has sent mixed signals, saying enforcement may have gone too far while naming hardliner Stephen Miller chief of staff.

Cabot Phillips explains that the Justice Department announced its largest anti-scam enforcement surge, tracing back to a March executive order from President Trump. Prosecutors have brought more than 400 cases against over 800 defendants in 85 districts, and Attorney General Todd Blanche says over 8 billion dollars in intended losses was recovered. Many scam workers are themselves trafficking victims held in compounds overseas, and the FBI's Operation Blackout has dismantled at least 29 compounds and freed more than 2,200 people. At home, seniors are the main targets, with cases including a Mexican list broker selling elderly Americans' details and Georgia prison gang members posing as jury duty officials. One mother described wiring over 5,000 dollars after hearing an apparent AI clone of her daughter's voice. The FBI has warned over 11,000 Americans and prevented at least 700 million dollars in losses.

The Army is urging residents within 100 miles of an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa to evacuate ahead of a planned 9 a.m. detonation of expiring bomb material. Combustion expert Dr. Ron Sawhoo explains the material is lead azide, stored for decades in an ethanol and water solution in 68 fifty-five-gallon drums in two earth-covered magazines. An inspection months ago found crystals forming, which can make it detonate from shock or vibration, so the Army wants to destroy it first. He describes several risks: the blast itself, lead that falls out, scattered lead azide, and toxic gases such as hydrazoic acid. Sheltering in place does not protect against gases, which can enter homes. Children and pregnant women are most vulnerable to lead. About 7,000 to 9,000 pounds of material is involved, and lead deposits could affect farmland and wells unless remediated.
